report.source_text: Given the worsening symptomatology due to the septic scenario sustained by empyema in the right pleural cavity, the patient was referred to a tertiary thoracic surgery department for management. A right thoracotomy surgery, with video-thoracoscopic assistance, was performed to remove the cyst, reduce the infectious burden, and perform a pleural debridement. Despite clinical improvement, a redo-surgery was necessary to repair a bronchopleural fistulation one week later. After completely recovering the right pleuropulmonary side, the hydatid cyst on the left lung, which also ruptured into bronchioles, was treated surgically using a total minimally invasive technique (Figure 2). The patient was discharged on postoperative day 23 after the first operation.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Cystic echinococcosis (CE) caused by Echinococcus granulosus sensu stricto (s.s.), G1 genotype, with pulmonary and hepatic involvement
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 43-year-old woman born in Romania and living in Sardinia, Italy for 23 years with occupational exposure to farm animals (dogs and sheep) and consumption of unwashed vegetables presented to the emergency department with a 2-year history of progressive weight loss, intermittent fever, and abdominal distension, followed by acute presentation with chest pain, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, and fever. On admission, imaging (chest radiography and CT) revealed two cystic lesions in the lungs and one giant cyst (16 cm) in the liver, staged as CE3a by WHO criteria. Laboratory findings showed leukocytosis (11,520 WBCs/μL), marked eosinophilia (53.3%), and elevated CRP (18.45 mg/dL). Serological testing (ELISA and Western Blot IgG) confirmed Echinococcus spp. antibodies. Molecular RT-PCR analysis of surgical specimens confirmed E. granulosus sensu stricto, G1 genotype. The patient developed a septic scenario with empyema in the right pleural cavity, requiring right thoracotomy with video-thoracoscopic assistance, followed by redo-surgery one week later for bronchopleural fistula repair, and minimally invasive surgery for the left lung cyst. Three weeks after lung surgery, the patient underwent PAIR (percutaneous aspiration, injection, re-aspiration) ultrasound-guided needle alcoholization of the liver cyst. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 23 with complete recovery and no signs of local recurrence at one week and one month follow-up.
